Decentralized CAR-T production: clinical, economic, and regulatory perspectives. Worldwide Network for Blood & Marrow Transplantation (WBMT) special article
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies and is rapidly expanding into solid tumors and autoimmune diseases. However, its full clinical potential remains constrained by centralized manufacturing, production costs, logistical complexity, prolonged vein-to-vein times, limited global accessibility, and regulatory frameworks that hinder rapid implementation of manufacturing innovations. Decentralized point-of-care manufacturing, pioneered by academic and clinical centers, offers a promising alternative to address these limitations and broaden patient access. This review summarizes the current landscape of POC CAR T-cell manufacturing, emphasizing clinical outcomes, economic sustainability, and regulatory considerations. Program experience across North America, Europe, Asia, and other regions demonstrates manufacturing innovations that reduce production times from several weeks to as few as 6-8 days. Early clinical studies report safety and efficacy comparable to commercially manufactured products while substantially lowering costs, with some models targeting production expenses of approximately USD 40,000 per treatment (excluding building and maintaining the production facility). We also examine supportive policy initiatives and regulatory pathways, including hospital exemption models, together with implementation challenges such as manufacturing heterogeneity, quality assurance, and workforce development. Finally, we discuss emerging technologies, including allogeneic CAR T-cell platforms, artificial intelligence-driven manufacturing, and in vivo gene editing, that may democratize global access.

title: Retrospective single center assessment of the new EBMT weighed score to predict SOS/VOD in pediatric HSCT
abstract: Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease (SOS/VOD) still represents one of the most challenging early complications after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), associated with high morbidity and mortality [ 1 , 2 ]. Defibrotide (DF) is approved for SOS/VOD treatment, whereas its prophylactic use is beyond the approved indications of the drug. In recent years, DF has been used as prophylaxis, as per institutional policy, in patients considered at highest risk, although universally shared criteria for identification of eligible patients are still lacking [ 3 , 4 , 5 ].

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome in young adults: A retrospective study on behalf of the EBMT Chronic Malignancies Working Party
authors: On behalf of the Chronic Malignancies Working Party of the EBMT
abstract: Abstract Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) in young adults are uncommon and underrepresented in transplant cohorts. We evaluated 697 patients aged 18–40 years who underwent first allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) reported to the EBMT between 2016 and 2021. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS); secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR), non-relapse mortality (NRM), and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). With a median follow-up of 2.8 years, 3-year OS and PFS were 69% (95% CI, 65–73) and 62% (58–66), respectively. At 3 years, CIR and NRM were 20% (16–23) and 18% (15–21). Grade II–IV acute GVHD occurred in 28% (25–32) by day +100, while chronic GVHD and extensive chronic GVHD occurred in 38% (34–42) and 18% (14–21) at 3 years. In multivariable analysis, very-poor cytogenetic risk was associated with inferior OS (HR 2.81, 95% CI 1.77–4.45). Haploidentical donors and reduced-intensity conditioning were also associated with inferior survival. Patients younger than 30 years had superior PFS, whereas outcomes with matched sibling and matched unrelated donors were comparable. These findings support the feasibility of allo-HCT in young adults with MDS and may help inform risk-adapted transplant approaches.

title: ATG exposure in T replete transplant for hematological malignancies: Real world analysis from BMT CTN 1202
abstract: Traditional weight-based dosing results in variable rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin (rATG) clearance, delaying CD4 + Tcell-immune-reconstitution (CD4 + IR) and impacting outcomes. In a retrospective pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of patients undergoing first T-replete hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), enrolled on BMT CTN 1202, we estimated post-HCT rATG-exposures as area under the curve (arbitrary unit per day/milliliter [AUxd/mL]) using a validated pharmacokinetic-model. Results were compared to patients who did not receive rATG. Previously defined post-HCT rATG-exposure groups: A:<30, B:30-55 and C:≥55 AUxd/mL were correlated with outcomes of interest using cox-proportional-hazard and cause-specific-hazards models. 325 patients (median age 51 years) were included: 228 received rATG. Median post-HCT rATG-exposure was 44.1 (Range 6.2-125.0). Among patients who received rATG, higher exposure correlated with worse five-year overall survival (OS) (no-ATG:51%; group A:67%; B:49%; C:34%, p = 0.01), higher five-year relapse incidence (no-ATG:31%; A:27%; B: 42%; C: 58%, p < 0.001) and lower CD4 + IR (no-ATG:64%; A:73%; B:51%; C:19%, p = 0.001). Grade 2-4 acute graft versus host disease (GVHD) rates were: no-ATG:40%; A:26%, B:39%, C:35%, (p = 0.44). Any rATG-exposure was associated with lower moderate/severe chronic GVHD (HR:0.63, p = 0.025). Low post-HCT rATG-exposure (< 30AUxd/mL) but not absent correlated with higher OS, lower relapse, and lower GVHD related deaths. Model-based-dosing could be used to target optimal post-HCT rATG-exposure and improve HCT outcomes.

Efficacy and safety of the ROCK2-inhibitor belumosudil for chronic GVHD: results from a multicenter retrospective analysis of a large German-Austrian cohort of the belumosudil MAP
abstract: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) is a significant risk factor for late morbidity and mortality after allogeneic stem cell transplantation. In Europe, so far there were no standard treatment options available after failure of corticosteroids and ruxolitinib. The selective ROCK-2 inhibitor belumosudil, a novel FDA-, and recently EMA-approved agent, has shown efficacy in phase-2 trials and had been made available to German and Austrian patients within a managed-access program (MAP). In a retrospective multicenter study, we analyzed 144 patients with predominately severe chronic GvHD (72%) receiving belumosudil within the MAP after a median of four prior therapeutic agents. The objective response rate at one and six months was partial remission or better in 53 and 52 patients (37% and 56%). Responses were observed across all organ systems. Median time to response was 1.3 months. At six months, steroids could be discontinued in 35% and reduced in 33% of patients. Failure-free survival was 81.9% and 75.8% at six and nine months. Six months overall survival was 96.9%. Treatment-emergent adverse reactions CTCAE grade III-IV were mostly infectious complications and occurred in 28 patients (22%). This retrospective analysis of a large real-world cohort demonstrates efficacy and safety of belumosudil in refractory chronic GvHD patients.

title: BEAM versus EAM, FEAM, BeEAM, and TEAM: exploring conditioning strategies in autologous stem cell transplantation for Hodgkin lymphoma a retrospective study of the LWP of EBMT
abstract: BEAM (carmustine, etoposide, cytarabine, and melphalan) remains the most used chemotherapy for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in chemosensitive relapsed Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). Nevertheless, alternatives have been developed to overcome drugs availability, costs, or potential toxicities. These include BeEAM (substitute carmustine with bendamustine), FEAM (using fotemustine instead of carmustine), TEAM (incorporating thiotepa instead of carmustine) and EAM (without bendamustine, fotemustine, thiotepa or carmustine). We analysed 13207 adults with HL who underwent HSCT in EBMT centers from 2010 to 2022. Chemotherapy was BEAM in 77% (n = 10167), FEAM in 13% (n = 1702), BeEAM in 6% (n = 729), TEAM in 3% (n = 365), and EAM in 2% (n = 244). In multivariable analysis, BeEAM was associated with decreased overall survival (OS) (HR 1.61, p = 0.003) and progression free survival (PFS) (HR 1.48, p < 0.001), higher relapse incidence (RI) (HR 1.43, p < 0.001) and non-relapse mortality (NRM) (HR 1.85, p = 0.04). EAM regimen was also associated with decreased OS (HR 1.55, p = 0.019). Propensity score matching was performed as a sensitivity analysis and confirmed the results of the multivariable analysis. We observed poorer outcomes in patients who received bendamustine in our cohort.

title: GvHD prophylaxis in elderly patients: post-transplant cyclophosphamide or ATG? A study by the EBMT transplant complications working party
abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo‑HCT) has become increasingly feasible in older patients with hematologic malignancies, yet the optimal graft‑versus‑host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis in this population remains uncertain. We compared post‑transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) with anti‑thymocyte globulin (ATG) in patients aged ≥60 years undergoing reduced‑intensity conditioning (RIC) peripheral blood stem cell allo‑HCT, using EBMT registry data from 2016 to 2022. A total of 7507 patients were included: 1418 matched sibling donors (MSD), 5051 matched unrelated donors (MUD), and 1038 mismatched unrelated donor (MMUD) transplants. In MSD recipients aged >65 years, PTCy was associated with reduced relapse, improved progression‑free survival (PFS), and superior GvHD‑ and relapse‑free survival (GRFS). However, in MSD recipients aged 60-65 years, these outcomes did not differ significantly between PTCy and ATG. Among MUD recipients, PTCy was associated with lower relapse and chronic GvHD, and a higher PFS, GRFS, and overall survival. In MMUD transplants, outcomes were not significantly different. Our findings indicate that PTCy is a safe and effective alternative to ATG in older allo‑HCT recipients, especially in MUD transplants and in MSD recipients aged >65 years, but the findings should be interpreted cautiously given their observational nature and patient heterogeneity. Further studies are warranted to assess long‑term outcomes.

Itacitinib plus calcineurin inhibitor–based therapy for prophylaxis of graft-versus-host disease: GRAVITAS-119 results
abstract: Abstract GRAVITAS-119 (NCT03320642), a single-arm, open-label, phase 1, proof-of-concept study, assessed addition of itacitinib to standard-of-care graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis regimens in reduced-intensity conditioning peripheral blood allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Day 28 hematologic recovery (percentage of patients demonstrating neutrophil recovery and platelet recovery) was the primary endpoint. Of 84 enrolled patients, 41 received itacitinib plus tacrolimus/methotrexate (nine with antithymocyte globulin [ATG]), 24 received itacitinib plus cyclosporine A/mycophenolate mofetil (16 with ATG), and 19 received itacitinib plus post-transplant cyclophosphamide/tacrolimus. Hematologic recovery was achieved by 51/55 (92.7%) evaluable patients (neutrophil recovery, 98.7%; platelet recovery, 94.6%). Estimated 1-year GVHD-free, relapse-free survival was 39.7%; estimated 1-year overall survival was 78.3%. Cumulative incidences for grade 2‒4 and grade 3‒4 acute GVHD at Day 180 were 13.2% and 4.8%, respectively; cumulative incidence of chronic GVHD at 1 year was 37.8%. Most common grade ≥ 3 adverse events were cytopenias; grade ≥ 3 infections occurred in 23 (27.4%) patients. Most patients receiving itacitinib plus standard-of-care GVHD prophylaxis achieved hematologic recovery, with any-grade GVHD and infection rates similar to previous reports with standard-of-care prophylaxis. Addition of itacitinib to GVHD prophylaxis permits timely hematologic recovery and does not increase GVHD or infection rates, although unmet need still remains for improved regimens.

title: Narsoplimab in critically ill patients with high-risk transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy requiring intensive care
Hyperacute Graft-Versus-Host Disease
abstract: Hyperacute graft-versus-host disease (HA-GVHD) is a fulminant form of acute GVHD that develops early after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, before neutrophil engraftment ensues, and is associated with increased risk of non-relapse mortality. While incidence of HA-GVHD appears to be decreasing owing to in vivo or ex vivo T-cell depletion strategies, it still contributes with life-threatening side effects in the setting of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatch or T-cell replete grafts with insufficient immune prophylaxis. Clinically, HA-GVHD presents almost always with severe skin involvement accompanied by fever, rash, diarrhea, and hepatic dysfunction. Differential diagnosis includes engraftment syndrome, adverse drug reactions, immunogenic skin reactions, and infectious exanthems. Therapeutic approaches mirror those prescribed for post-transplant acute GVHD, centered on high-dose systemic corticosteroids. Although there is no consensus on managing corticosteroid-refractory cases, ruxolitinib could be considered the therapy of choice based on data from post-engraftment GVHD. Further studies are needed to assess effectiveness of novel agents in corticosteroid-refractory HA-GVHD. The main purpose of this review is to summarize available literature on pathophysiology, incidence, risk factors, differential diagnosis, and treatment considerations for HA-GVHD. Knowledge gaps, particularly pertaining to use of post-transplant cyclophosphamide and treatment of corticosteroid-refractory HA-GVHD, are emphasized to highlight future research opportunities.

title: Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: Risk factors and longitudinal pulmonary function trajectories in a multicenter cohort
abstract: Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (PPFE) is an uncommon but serious late pulmonary complication after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), frequently resulting in the need for lung transplantation and contributing substantially to mortality. However, its risk factors and prediagnostic pulmonary function trajectory remain poorly defined. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 1818 patients who underwent allogeneic HSCT between 2005 and 2023. PPFE was diagnosed using established clinical criteria. Cumulative incidence was estimated treating death as a competing event, risk factors were evaluated using cause-specific Cox models, and prediagnostic pulmonary function trajectories were analyzed using mixed-effects and segmented regression models. During a median follow-up of 42.5 months, 306 patients developed late-onset noninfectious pulmonary complications (LONIPCs), including 19 with PPFE. Although the overall incidence of LONIPCs did not differ by graft source, umbilical cord blood transplantation (UCBT) was associated with higher cumulative incidence of PPFE. In an adjusted cause-specific Cox analysis, UCBT remained associated with PPFE, whereas chronic graft-versus-host disease was not significantly associated. PPFE occurred late after transplantation and was preceded by accelerated %FVC decline approximately four years before clinical diagnosis. These findings suggest that extended pulmonary function surveillance may support earlier detection of PPFE in selected high-risk HSCT recipients.

title: Bridging therapy in pediatric and AYA patients under 25 years with relapsed/refractory B-ALL undergoing anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy: a multicenter retrospective study by the Spanish group GETH-TC
abstract: CAR-T therapy is a powerful treatment for pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). However, the impact of bridging therapy prior to CAR-T infusion on patient outcomes remains insufficiently explored. In this retrospective study of patients with relapse/refractory B-ALL (N = 103), we compared outcomes across different bridging therapy groups: Low-Intensity Chemotherapy (LIC, N = 50), Immunotherapy (N = 20), or High-Intensity Chemotherapy (HIC, N = 33). At day +28 post-infusion, LIC and Immunotherapy showed significantly higher rates of Complete Remission with negative Minimal Residual Disease compared with HIC (96% vs 85% vs 75%), along with lower rates of disease progression (4% vs 10% vs 15.2%) and treatment-related mortality (0% vs 5% vs 9.1%). Additionally, patients who received three or more prior lines of therapy before CAR-T infusion exhibited significantly lower response rates. Despite potential biases, such as intrinsic disease aggressiveness or unidentified genomic alterations, present findings suggest that using LIC or immunotherapy as bridging strategies, in patients with fewer prior treatment lines, may be associated with a lower overall disease and treatment burden and could potentially contribute to improved CAR-T cell efficacy and clinical outcomes. Nevertheless, additional investigations are required to elucidate biological and clinical mechanisms by which bridging approaches and treatment history modulate CAR-T responses.

The prognostic impact of CEBPA mutation in acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
abstract: The presence of mutations in basic leucine zipper (bZIP) region of the CEBPA gene in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is defined as a favorable risk marker according to the guidelines. A total of 173 CEBPA-mutated AML patients receiving allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) were retrospectively recruited, compared with 345 control patients selected by propensity score matching. Patients carrying CEBPA mut had a better 5-year PFS than CEBPA wt group (60.8% vs. 55.0%, P = 0.016). Failure to achieve complete remission after first induction chemotherapy, the presence of CEBPA mutation before allo-HSCT and the absence of maintenance therapy were proven to be statistically significant factors for worse survival (all P in-frame bZIP 59.9% vs. CEBPA no in-frame bZIP 63.3% vs. CEBPA wt 55.0%, P = 0.045; CEBPA mut /FLT3-ITD mut 75.9% vs. CEBPA mut /FLT3-ITD wt 57.3% vs. CEBPA wt 55.0%, P = 0.02). Conversely, the presence of GATA2 mutations showed no benefit. Our findings suggest that CEBPA mut patients with nontypical in-frame shift in bZIP region or with the co-mutation of FLT3-ITD could benefit from allo-HSCT.

title: How could calreticulin-targeting therapies change the myelofibrosis transplant paradigm?
abstract: Abstract Myelofibrosis (MF), the most severe Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm, is driven by mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL, with CALR mutations accounting for 30–35% of cases. Mutant CALR forms an aberrant complex with the thrombopoietin receptor, resulting in constitutive JAK–STAT signalling and is expressed on the malignant cell surface as a tumour-specific neoantigen absent from normal tissues, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) remains the only curative treatment but is limited to selected patients with adequate fitness and a suitable donor. This review summarises the rapidly evolving landscape of CALR-directed therapies, including peptide vaccines, the Fc-silenced monoclonal antibody INCA033989, bispecific T-cell engagers, antibody-drug conjugates, and the CAR T-cell therapy RPG4, and explores their potential impact on transplant decision-making. INCA033989 has generated the most mature clinical data, demonstrating improvements in splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, anaemia and early markers of disease modification, whereas cytotoxic approaches such as CAR T-cell therapy offer the prospect of deeper clonal eradication. Collectively, these therapies have the potential to redefine the role and timing of allo-HCT and expand treatment opportunities in the peri-transplant setting, including the targeted eradication of measurable residual disease following transplantation.

title: A multimodal approach to sexual function after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Sexual dysfunction is a frequent long-term complication following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). This multicenter, prospective, randomized controlled trial evaluated the feasibility and efficacy of a multimodal intervention targeting sexual function and early detection of genital chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) in adult recipients of HSCT. Participants were randomized 1:1 to the intervention or usual care. The intervention included repeated questionnaires, genital assessments, and nurse-led consultations. Sexual function was assessed using the Female Sexual Function Index or the International Index of Erectile Function, with secondary outcomes including sexual health, sexual distress, and feasibility measures. Overall sexual function did not differ significantly between groups for women (difference (diff) 3.3, P = 0.391) or men (diff 0.9, P = 0.761). Significant improvements favoring the intervention group were observed in women's sexual pain (diff -2.1, P = 0.019) and, for both sexes, in sexual pain (diff -13.6, P = 0.030), communication with professionals (diff -15.5, P = 0.017), and partnership quality (diff -22.8, P = 0.040). The incidence of genital cGVHD was 25.0% among male (n = 11) and 28.1% (n = 9) among females. We conclude that the multimodal intervention was feasible, led to improved sexual health, and facilitated earlier recognition of genital cGVHD, supporting the integration of interdisciplinary sexual health assessments into routine post-HSCT care.

title: Lung transplantation after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: a study from the Transplant Complications Working Party of the EBMT
abstract: Late-onset non-infectious pulmonary complications (LONIPCs) are severe late complications after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), associated with high morbidity and mortality. Lung transplantation (LT) may offer a survival benefit, but is infrequently performed due to concerns regarding outcomes. We conducted a retrospective multicenter study of adult patients who underwent LT for LONIPCs after HCT between 2000 and 2019. Thirty-one centers contributed clinical data. Seventy-one patients were included (59% male). Median age at HCT was 31 years. Acute leukemia was the most common HCT indication (62%). Peripheral blood was the main stem cell source (87%), and related donors accounted for 54% of cases. All patients developed chronic graft-versus-host disease, severe in 78%, with lung involvement in 88%. Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome was the primary indication for LT (78%), occurring a median of 55 months after HCT. Bilateral LT was performed in 93% of cases. Overall survival at 1 and 5 years after LT was 87% and 71%, respectively. HLA-mismatched donor transplantation and corticosteroid use at LT were associated with inferior survival. LT is a feasible option for selected patients with end-stage LONIPCs, with long-term survival comparable to that reported for LT performed for other indications.

title: The role of palliative and supportive care in haematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapy. Recommendations from the EBMT practice harmonisation and guidelines committee
abstract: Haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) and cellular therapies (CT), including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, offer curative potential for patients with haematologic malignancies but are associated with substantial physical, psychological, social and existential burden. Despite growing evidence that early integration of palliative and supportive care improves quality of life (QoL), symptom control, communication, and decision-making, its implementation remains heterogeneous and often delayed. This EBMT Practice Harmonisation and Guidelines paper was developed using a structured expert-consensus process. An international multidisciplinary panel of clinicians with expertise in adult and paediatric HCT, CT and palliative care conducted targeted literature reviews and discussions to generate pragmatic, non-graded recommendations. Recommendations address key domains across the HCT and CT continuum, including symptom management, psychological distress, graft-versus-host disease, relapse, end-of-life care, advance care planning, caregiver support, health inequities, and healthcare professional factors. Evidence supports early, integrated palliative care to reduce symptom burden, improve QoL, and facilitate complex decision-making. Practical referral triggers, incorporation of patient-reported outcomes, and parallel planning are proposed to promote timely and equitable access. Palliative and supportive care should be systematically integrated throughout HCT and CT. These EBMT recommendations provide a framework to support holistic, person-centred care and harmonise clinical practice.

title: Pre-transplant immunotherapy and MRD dynamics affect post-transplant prognosis in KMT2A-rearranged B-ALL patients
abstract: To explore factors affecting post-transplant outcomes in patients with KMT2A-rearranged (KMT2A-r) B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), we performed a retrospective study including 44 newly diagnosed KMT2A-r B-ALL patients treated at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University from 2018 to 2025. KMT2A-r and MFC-MRD were assessed at four time points: post-induction (MRD1), post-first consolidation (MRD2), post-second consolidation (MRD3), and pre-transplant (MRD4). Incorporation of immunotherapy (CAR-T or blinatumomab) into induction and consolidation regimens enhanced remission depth at all MRD1 to MRD4 time points. Immunotherapy bridging to transplantation was associated with superior overall survival (OS) compared with direct transplantation (P = 0.03), with a trend toward longer median relapse-free survival (RFS) of 39.0 (95% CI: 3.9-74.1) vs. 5.0 (95% CI: 1.6-8.4) months (P = 0.10). In addition, the cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR) was lower in the immunotherapy bridging to transplantation group (P = 0.02). KMT2A-r and MFC-MRD negativity peaked pre-transplant. Four dynamic patterns were identified; sustained or converted negativity correlated with better prognosis, and sustained positivity with poor outcomes. Multivariate analysis revealed that sustained KMT2A positivity and the absence of pre-transplant immunotherapy were independent adverse risk factors. In conclusion, first-line immunotherapy yields deeper remission; immunotherapy bridging to transplantation is superior; dynamic KMT2A-r and MFC-MRD strongly predict post-transplant prognosis.

Metabolic pathways as therapeutic target to improve allo-HSCT outcomes
abstract: Abstract Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) remains the only curative option for many high-risk hematologic malignancies, yet its efficacy is limited by graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), relapse, and immune dysregulation. Emerging evidence identifies cellular metabolism as a central, underexplored determinant of transplant outcomes. Across transplant-relevant malignancies, including myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukemia, and high-risk lymphoma, disease-specific metabolic programs encompassing mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, lipid and fatty acid remodeling, and oncometabolite accumulation cooperate to sustain clonal persistence, suppress antitumor immunity, and confer resistance to cytotoxic and targeted therapies. Within the transplant itself, donor T-cell metabolic reprogramming fuels the dichotomy between GVHD and graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) activity, with alloreactive effector T cells depending on glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation in ways that are mechanistically separable from GVL-mediating responses. This review synthesizes current evidence on disease-specific and transplant-specific metabolic programs and evaluates pharmacological strategies that may be deployed peri-transplant to simultaneously reduce GVHD, prevent relapse, and preserve GVL.

title: The first attempts to transplant bone marrow—tribute to Jan Raszek-Rosenbusch and Franciszek Groër.
abstract: Bone marrow transplantation is now a mature therapeutic method, but it was developed over many years and started from the idea that bone marrow may contain some factors of curative potential and thus could be used as a medicine for blood disorders. The first attempts to administer bone marrow in a manner allowing (at least theoretically) its engraftment are usually assigned to Edwin E. Osgood and collaborators from Oregon University [ 1 ], who reported in 1939 that they had transfused intravenously bone marrow to a patient with aplastic anemia who died five days later. Little attention is being paid to the attempts described in 1949 (but carried out in the years 1938–1941) by Jan Raszek-Rosenbusch (later using Raszek as the only surname) and Franciszek Groër to administer bone marrow intramedullary in King John Casimir University in Lwow, Poland (now Lviv, Ukraine) [ 2 ]. While performed in the years when knowledge of hematology and the physiological role of the bone marrow was still in its infancy, these attempts had the objective of transfusing with the bone marrow “‘unknown, but necessary biological factors. responsible for the normal structure and functioning of the hematopoietic system.” Donors and recipients were matched for ABO blood groups and were unrelated. Donors were usually adults, and recipients were children. Several milliliters of bone marrow were aspirated from the sternum of the donor and immediately injected into the sternum of the recipient. Procedures were repeated on the same recipients several times. No immediate or delayed toxicity with this procedure was observed, while some improvements in general condition were reported. These improvements are difficult to comment on because of uncertainties in matching the diagnoses reported (unspecified anemia with jaundice and “lymphadenosis aleukemica”) with contemporary nomenclature. Of course, there was no HLA match, no conditioning, no chimerism studies performed, and the description of the effects did not conform to today's standards. So this was only an attempt to transplant, and not yet a transplantation. Interestingly, the reported clinical attempts by Raszek-Rosenbusch were apparently preceded by experiments on rabbits, but the only document to confirm this is a photo (Fig. 1 ) from 1938 showing four doctors and two anesthetized rabbits. According to late Irena Raszek (sister of Jan) they drilled a hole using dentist drill in the head of femoral bone of one rabbit, collected bone marrow and injected it into femoral bone of another rabbit. After finding that rabbits easily survive this procedure, they have started clinical trials. Besides original publication by Raszek-Rosenbusch [ 2 ], more recently a movie was found [ 3 ] prepared by Soviet authorities most likely in 1940 when they transiently occupied Lwow at the beginning of WWII. Excerpts from this movie are shown as Fig. 2 . As shown, Professor Groër is first pointing to two people lying side by side: a child (recipient on the right) and an adult (donor on the left). Then Dr. Raszek is inserting a sternal needle into a child and is checking that the needle is really in the marrow cavity. Then one can see a needle in the sternum of the donor. Subsequently, Dr. Raszek is aspirating marrow from the donor and then injecting this marrow into the recipient. Finally, Professor Groër, Dr. Raszek, and the third doctor of unknown identity congratulate the recipient. As shown on the timer at the bottom of the screen, the entire procedure took approximately one minute and was very different from the contemporary technique. The intramedullary route was chosen because it was not known at the time that marrow components from the donor might reach the recipient’s marrow when infused intravenously. The identity of the other doctors in the photo is unknown. Fig. 2: Excerpts from the Soviet movie from 1940 in occupied Lwow. Then Dr. Raszek-Rosenbusch is checking that the needle is properly inserted into the sternum of the recipient. Subsequently, a needle in the sternum of the donor is shown, and as the next step, Dr. Raszek-Rosenbusch is collecting marrow from the donor. Finally, Dr. Raszek-Rosenbusch is injecting donor marrow into the recipient's intramedullary space. In the last photograph, Professor Groër, Dr. Raszek-Rosenbusch, and the third doctor of unknown identity congratulate the recipient.
